title: After Midnight
excerpt: Workplace Romance · Forbidden Attraction · Slow Burn · Mature Romance
content:
Three days passed.

Naomi and Devraj worked together as professionally as ever. They spoke about wine pairings, service timings, and the evening reservations. They exchanged no private messages, and neither mentioned the photograph.

But something had changed.

Naomi noticed it in the small things.

The coffee stopped appearing beside her station.

Devraj no longer lingered after service to help her count inventory. When their shifts ended, he said goodnight and left.

He wasn't punishing her.

He was giving her the space she had asked for.

Somehow, that made her miss him more.

On Thursday night, the restaurant hosted a private dinner for a group of investors. Every table was occupied, the kitchen was running behind, and one of the ovens decided to stop cooperating at precisely the wrong moment.

Naomi stood at the pass, issuing instructions while two cooks hurried to rescue a tray of vegetables.

"Table twelve needs the fish in six minutes!"

"Three minutes!" someone shouted.

"Then make it three!"

A server appeared with another problem.

Naomi turned, ready to answer, and found Devraj already there.

"I've moved the wine service for table twelve," he said. "They've agreed to wait while we finish the mains."

She looked at him.

"You did?"

"I spoke to them. They're happy with the pairing and a little extra time."

For a moment, she could only stare.

He had anticipated the problem before she had time to ask for help.

"Thank you," she said.

"Of course."

He started to leave.

"Devraj."

He paused.

She wanted to say everything then. She wanted to tell him that she missed the coffee, the conversations, and the way he looked at her when nobody else was watching.

Instead, she said, "Could you give me five minutes after service?"

His expression was careful.

"Yes."

The dinner ended successfully.

By midnight, the last guests had left, the tables were cleared, and the staff began their closing routines.

Naomi washed her hands, removed her apron, and walked toward the service corridor.

Devraj was waiting by the back door.

For a moment, neither spoke.

Then Naomi took a breath.

"I've been thinking."

"That sounds serious."

"It is."

He waited.

"I wrote that rule after someone hurt me. I thought if I made it absolute, I wouldn't have to worry about being hurt like that again."

Devraj's expression softened, but he didn't interrupt.

"I don't regret protecting myself. I regret assuming that protecting myself meant never taking a risk."

She looked down at her hands.

"I don't want to rush into anything. I don't want the restaurant to become a place where we fight about our relationship, and I don't want to feel as though I have to choose between you and the work I've spent years building."

"You shouldn't have to."

"I know. And I need you to understand that if we do this, my work matters. My independence matters. I need us to be honest, even when honesty is uncomfortable."

He nodded.

"Agreed."

"And if something goes wrong, we talk about it. We don't punish each other. We don't drag colleagues into it. We don't turn our private lives into gossip."

"Agreed."

She looked up.

"And I don't want you to disappear just because I'm scared."

His eyes held hers.

"Then tell me when you're scared. Don't make me guess."

She laughed softly, a little embarrassed.

"I'm trying."

"I can see that."

Silence settled between them.

Naomi took one step closer.

"I miss you."

The words came out quieter than she intended.

Devraj's face changed.

"I miss you too."

"I miss your stupid coffee."

"I can bring it back."

"And your terrible jokes."

"Those are complimentary."

"And the way you look at me when you think I'm not paying attention."

He smiled.

"That one might be difficult to stop."

Naomi shook her head, laughing.

Then the laughter faded.

"Can I kiss you?" she asked.

For once, Devraj was the one who looked surprised.

"Are you sure?"

"No," she admitted. "I'm nervous. I'm probably going to overthink it tomorrow. But I want to kiss you tonight."

He reached for her hand.

"Then come here."

She closed the distance between them.

Their kiss was gentle, familiar, and somehow more meaningful than the first. There was no wine room, no accidental closeness, and no convenient excuse to pretend it hadn't happened.

Naomi had chosen it.

When they drew apart, Devraj brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

"So," he said, "what happens to the rule?"

She smiled.

"I think it needs rewriting."

"That sounds promising."

"Don't get excited. I'm not putting up a public announcement."

"Wouldn't dream of it."

She leaned against his shoulder.

For a little while, they stood together in the quiet corridor, listening to the kitchen settle around them.

Then Naomi straightened.

"There's something else."

"Should I be worried?"

"Possibly."

She took his hand and led him toward the kitchen pass.

The restaurant was empty. The stainless-steel counters reflected the soft overhead lights, and the familiar smell of herbs and warm bread lingered in the air.

Naomi opened the drawer beneath her station and removed the folded piece of paper.

Her old rule.

She smoothed it against the counter.

Then she took a fresh sheet from her notebook and wrote:

No relationship is worth losing yourself for.

She paused, thinking.

Beneath it, she added:

But fear doesn't get to make every decision.

Devraj read the words over her shoulder.

"I like that."

"It's a work in progress."

"Most good things are."

She looked at him, and her smile turned mischievous.

"You know what else is a work in progress?"

"What?"

"Our first dinner. I still think six courses was excessive."

"It was five."

"You told me six."

"I was trying to impress you."

"Well, it nearly worked."

He laughed and drew her into another kiss.

This one lasted long enough for Naomi to forget whatever clever response she had planned.

When they finally separated, she rested her forehead against his.

"Walk me home?"

"Every time you ask."

"And coffee tomorrow?"

"Already planned."

She smiled.

"Good."

Outside, the city was quiet, and midnight had passed without either of them noticing.

They left the restaurant hand in hand, not knowing exactly what the next week would bring, but no longer pretending that uncertainty was a reason to walk away.

Behind them, the kitchen stood empty.

Above the pass, the old rule was gone.

And for Naomi, that was not the end of a promise.

It was the beginning of a different one.

To be continued…
